docs.title: DEE Debugger for VS Code — User Guide
docs.text:
Develop Critical Manufacturing MES DEE Actions in VS Code, against a running MES — with the full editor and a real debugger instead of the MES web UI's small code box.

What it does:

  • Browse every DEE Action in the MES from a tree view.
  • Edit any action as a normal .cs file, with full C# IntelliSense.
  • Upload changes back to the MES — compile errors show inline in the editor.
  • Debug live — set breakpoints and step through your action while the MES host runs it. (The headline feature.)
  • Sync your whole action portfolio against a git-tracked customization project.

It works whether the MES host runs as a local Docker container, inside a devcontainer, on a remote machine, in Kubernetes/OpenShift, or as a plain local process — and succeeds the "Critical Manufacturing DEE Explorer" Visual Studio add-in, rebuilt for VS Code.

What is a DEE Action?

A DEE Action (DEE = Dynamic Execution Engine) is a C# business rule stored in the MES database, not compiled into a customization DLL. Each attaches to an Action Group — an extension point like MaterialManagement.MaterialManagementOrchestration.CreateMaterial.Pre — and the host compiles and runs it on the fly when that operation happens. Because the code lives in the database, you'd normally edit it in the MES web UI; this extension gives you VS Code and a debugger instead.

Development and test environments only

The debugging and upload features are for dev/test only. Never attach a debugger to, or enable DEE debug mode on, a production MES. See the FAQ.

docs.title: Where things live in VS Code
docs.text:
• Getting Started walkthrough — DEE Debugger: Open Getting Started (also Help → Welcome) walks through connect → authenticate → open → debug → sync with a button per step. The fastest first contact with the extension.
  • DEE Explorer — the tree view in the DEE Debugger icon on the Activity Bar (left edge of the window). Its title bar holds Refresh, New DEE Action…, Filter and Attach Debugger (plus VS Code's own Collapse All); everything else (Switch Environment, Sync, Expand All, Show Disabled Actions, Show Output Log, Collect Support Bundle, Open Getting Started) is under the … menu. On a row, hover for the inline actions and right-click for the full menu, including Open in MES UI.
  • Command Palette — press Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS) and type "DEE Debugger" to see every command.
  • Status bar — the MES: <environment> item shows which environment you are connected to (and how many actions are in debug mode); click it to switch. Routine confirmations such as saved to MES also appear there briefly.
  • DEE Debugger output channel — View → Output, then pick DEE Debugger in the dropdown. This is the first place to look when something fails; see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Debugging DEE actions
docs.text: Warning: DEE debug mode and debugger attach are for development and test environments only. Attaching a debugger to a host is highly privileged, and a paused host stops the entire MES for everyone using it. The extension warns you before attaching to a non-local address; treat that warning seriously.

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text:
Understand this first — everything else about debugging follows from it.

When you enable DEE debug mode for an action, the MES host stops using the code stored in its database for you. Instead, every time you trigger the action, it compiles your local file (the extension delivers it into the host container) with debug symbols. Five consequences:

  1. It's per-user. The debug registration is keyed to the user your token belongs to. Only operations executed as that user run your file's code and can hit your breakpoints. Everyone else — colleagues, integrations, other accounts — keeps executing the normal database version, completely unaffected. This also means: if you trigger the action from the MES UI logged in as a different account, your breakpoint will never hit. See the FAQ.
  2. It's in-memory. The registration lives in the host process's memory. A host restart (container restart, stack recreate, redeploy) silently forgets it. The extension notices on the next DEE Explorer refresh and asks whether to re-enable — see host restarts.
  3. Hot reload, no save-to-MES needed. While debug mode is on, every time you save the file (Ctrl+S), the extension pushes it to the host, and your next execution compiles and runs the new code. You iterate — edit, save, trigger, inspect — without ever running Save Action to MES. The database version doesn't change until you explicitly save to MES.
  4. The database is untouched until you say so. Turning debug mode off returns you to the stored version instantly. If you like your changes, publish them with Save Action to MES (Compile & Save) — that's the moment they become real for all users.
  5. A paused host is a stopped MES. .NET debugging suspends the entire host process while stopped at a breakpoint. See everything freezes.

docs.title: Before your first debug session
docs.text:
• The Microsoft C# extension must be installed (it comes automatically with this extension).
  • Your environment must be able to reach the host container — if Enable DEE Debug Mode or Attach fail with container errors, fix the environment first.
  • Linux MES hosts up to 11.x need a one-time host-side fix. You don't have to remember it: the extension checks the host when you enable debug mode or attach and offers to apply the fix. MES 12 images already contain it. Background in the Linux host prerequisite.

docs.title: The debug loop, step by step
1. Toggle debug mode on
docs.text:
Right-click the action in the DEE Explorer → Enable DEE Debug Mode (or the bug icon on the row; the same entry reads Disable DEE Debug Mode while it is on — the Command Palette offers the state-agnostic Toggle DEE Debug Mode). The extension copies your local file into the host container, registers debug mode with the MES, and opens the file. The action gets a DEBUG badge and a bug icon, the status bar shows how many actions are in debug mode, and a dialog asks Attach the debugger now? (Attach Debugger / Not Now) — its detail text states the semantics (per-user, in-memory, hot reload). Set deeDebugger.attachAfterEnablingDebug to always or never to skip the question; it is never asked while the debugger is already attached.

(If the action has no local file yet, the extension downloads it first. For a DeeDevBase file, the working copy is what gets debugged. On a containerized host the extension also checks the Linux PDB prerequisite at this point — see below.)

docs.title: 2. Attach the debugger
docs.text:
Choose Attach Debugger in that dialog, or run DEE Debugger: Attach Debugger to MES Host (also the debug icon in the DEE Explorer's title bar) any time.

  • First time on a fresh container: the .NET debugger (vsdbg) isn't in the MES host image. The extension detects this and offers to install it (Install vsdbg) — say yes. On MES 12 hosts the image has curl, so it downloads inside the container (the container needs internet access). MES 11.x images have no download tool, so the extension downloads vsdbg on your machine and streams it into the container — that needs internet access plus bash and tar locally (on Windows, run VS Code in WSL).
  • The extension finds the MES host process automatically. If it ever shows a process picker instead, choose the dotnet process running Cmf.Foundation.Services.HostService.dll — not the CmfEntrypoint wrapper (PID 1), which can't be attached to.

You're attached when VS Code's debug toolbar appears and the extension shows "Attached to the MES host. …".

Kubernetes / OpenShift environments need two things in the host pod spec, because there is no privileged-exec workaround on clusters:

  • securityContext.capabilities.add: ["SYS_PTRACE"] on the host container;
  • since the host image runs as a non-root user (and added capabilities are dropped for non-root users), either runAsUser: 0 on that container or kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0 on the node.

The extension checks this before attaching and tells you exactly what is missing. See the per-type setup notes.

docs.title: 3. Set a breakpoint
docs.text:
Click in the gutter next to a line inside the action-code markers of your file.

Note: The breakpoint may show as a hollow circle (unbound) at first. That's normal — the debug-compiled assembly only loads when the action first executes. It fills in solid at that moment and hits.

docs.title: 4. Trigger the action
docs.text:
Make the MES execute the action as your user:

  • Perform the hooked operation in the MES UI, logged in as the same account your token belongs to — e.g. create a Material to hit a …CreateMaterial.Pre action; or
  • Right-click the action → Execute Action… for a direct run with a JSON input of your choosing (this always runs as your token's user). The execute call waits while you sit at the breakpoint; after 60 seconds the extension gives up on it and reports that it could not reach the MES host — with a hint that the host is probably paused.

The breakpoint hits: you can inspect Input and other locals, step, and continue.

docs.title: 5. Iterate
docs.text: Change the code inside the markers, save — the status bar flashes DEE: pushed … to host — and trigger again. The new code runs. No upload, no recompile step on your side.

docs.title: 6. Finish
docs.text:
• Happy with the change? Save Action to MES (Compile & Save) to publish it for everyone. See the save semantics.
  • Right-click → Disable DEE Debug Mode to turn debug off — the stored version takes over again for you. If you close the VS Code window with debug mode still on, the extension cleans up your registrations on the way out (best effort).
  • Disconnect the debugger with the debug toolbar's disconnect button (see below).

docs.title: Debug session controls (Continue, Disconnect, …)
docs.text:
Once attached, VS Code shows the debug toolbar. Because this is an attach session (you attached to the already-running MES host — you didn't launch it), the controls behave a little differently from launching an app. What each does:

Control Shortcut What it does here Continue F5 Resumes the host and keeps the debugger attached. Use this after a breakpoint — it un-freezes the MES so it (and your next trigger) can run. Pause — Manually suspends the host. Avoid on shared stacks — it freezes the whole MES. Step Over / Into / Out F10 / F11 / Shift+F11 Normal stepping while paused. Step Into can enter product Cmf.* code you have no source for ("no source available") — use Step Over to stay in your code. Disconnect (the red "stop" icon) Shift+F5 Ends the debug session by DETACHING — vsdbg lets go and the host keeps running. This is how you finish debugging. It does not stop or kill the MES host. Restart Ctrl+Shift+F5 Detaches and re-attaches. Rarely needed; if the host was restarted, just re-run Attach instead.

Always Disconnect (Shift+F5) when you're done — and don't leave the host paused

A debug session that ends uncleanly (you close the VS Code window or the WSL/remote connection drops while still attached, especially while paused) can leave the debugger attached with the host's request threads suspended. The host then answers / but every /api call hangs — the extension looks broken with "could not reach the MES host" timeouts. Killing the debugger process does not recover it; only restarting the host container does. So: Continue (F5) off any breakpoint before you step away, and Disconnect (Shift+F5) when finished rather than just closing the window.

The extension detaches its own attach sessions automatically when it shuts down normally, so a routine window close is safe — but a crash or dropped remote connection can still orphan the debugger. If you hit the "host answers but /api hangs" symptom, restart the MES host.

Disconnect vs. Disable DEE Debug Mode — two independent things:

  • Disconnect ends the debugger (vsdbg) session. Your DEE Debug Mode registration is untouched — the host still compiles your local file on the next trigger (the status bar keeps showing the 🐞 count as a reminder).
  • Disable DEE Debug Mode ends the host-side registration — the stored database version runs again. It does not detach the debugger.

Finishing a debug session cleanly usually means both: Disable DEE Debug Mode, then Disconnect.

docs.title: While you are paused, everything freezes
docs.text:
While the debugger has the host stopped — at a breakpoint, stepped, paused, or on an exception — the entire MES host process is suspended. The MES UI stops responding, API calls time out, colleagues on the same instance are blocked, and even this extension's own tree refreshes fail. This is normal .NET debugging behavior, not an outage.

Note: If you see "could not reach the MES host" errors while a debug session is active, the extension reminds you the host is probably paused. Press Continue (F5) and retry. And on a shared dev instance, be a good neighbor: don't stay paused for long.

docs.title: What happens when the host restarts
docs.text: Because debug registrations are in-memory, a host restart (someone recreated the stack, the container crashed, an install ran) drops them — while your local file, your DEBUG badge, and your attached session know nothing about it. The extension reconciles with the server on every refresh: when it finds your debug mode gone, it tells you debug mode was lost and offers to re-enable it. Accept, re-attach if needed, and carry on. (After a full stack recreate on a Linux host, you may also need to re-apply the PDB patch — next section.)

docs.title: Linux MES hosts: the PDB prerequisite
docs.text:
MES releases up to 11.x have a product bug (#158143) that breaks DEE debug mode on Linux-containerized hosts (the default for local stacks): the host generates debug symbols in a Windows-only format, so executing an action in debug mode fails with an error like the one below. MES 12 images already contain the fix; the probe described here simply reports them as fine.

The Action <name> code is invalid: … Unexpected error writing debug information --
'Value cannot be null. (Parameter 'type')'

On an affected host the extension can patch it for you: run DEE Debugger: Patch Host for DEE Debugging (dev/test)…. It flips the one setting in the host's Cmf.Foundation.Common.dll to emit the cross-platform PortablePdb format, backs up the original (.orig), and restarts the host. The patcher runs inside the container, under the host's own .NET runtime.

  • You are told up front. Before enabling debug mode on a containerized host, and before attaching, the extension probes the host (a read-only run of the bundled patcher) and, if the host still emits Windows-only symbols, asks Patch Host for Debugging / Continue Anyway. Without this, the failure happens out of sight: you trigger the action from the MES UI, the host fails to compile the debug build, and your breakpoint simply never binds. The attach-time warning does not block (custom-business DLL breakpoints need no patch), and the "breakpoints have not bound" notice also carries the patch button when the host is known to be unpatched. Set deeDebugger.hostPatchCheck to off to skip the probe.
  • When a debug execute fails with the error above, the error notification offers a Patch Host for Debugging… button directly.
  • It's a dev/test-only action (it modifies a product assembly). Run directly, the command asks you to confirm (Patch host); from one of the prompts above, your click counts as that confirmation. The same non-local-host warning as attach applies.
  • Docker / docker-in-docker hosts are restarted automatically; on Kubernetes / OpenShift the command patches and then tells you the rollout restart to run.
  • Undo any time with Restore Host DLL (undo debug patch)….
  • Set deeDebugger.hostAppDir if your host keeps the app somewhere other than /opt/app.

Note: The patch lives in the container's writable layer. Recreating the stack (cmf dev local stack down / up) reverts it — just run the patch command again. A plain restart keeps the patch but clears debug registrations (previous section). The manual tools/host-pdb-patcher tool remains for scripted/CI use.

docs.title: Load-balanced environments
docs.text:
If the environment runs several host instances behind a load balancer, your debug registration and your attach both live on one instance — but the balancer may send executions to another, where the stored version runs and no breakpoint exists. Point your environment's host address directly at a single instance while debugging.

On Kubernetes/OpenShift this is the default posture whenever the host deployment has more than one replica — four things must land on the same replica (the activation call, the pushed file, the trigger, and the attached debugger). Either scale to one replica while debugging (kubectl scale deployment/host --replicas=1 -n <namespace>) or pin everything to one pod with kubectl port-forward — the recipe and a diagram of the failure mode are in How debugging works.

docs.title: Attaching for custom business debugging
docs.text:
Everything above debugs DEE Actions — C# rules stored in the MES database. But an MES customization also has custom business projects: Cmf.Custom.<tenant>.* code compiled into DLLs and deployed into the host image (Cmf.Custom.Business is only the folder holding Business.sln — the assemblies themselves carry the tenant in the name).

The same command debugs both. DEE Debugger: Attach Debugger to MES Host attaches the stock coreclr debugger to the MES host once, with a source map that covers both DEE temp files and your deployed business DLLs — so a breakpoint binds wherever the matching code runs. You no longer choose "which attach"; you attach and set breakpoints where you need them. For the full contrast see DEE vs custom-business debugging.

Breakpoint in… Binds against Source map (merged automatically) Edit loop A DEE Action the host-compiled local file (Debug Mode on) the DEE temp folder live-compile — edit, save, re-trigger A Cmf.Custom.<tenant>.* DLL the deployed assembly the paths recorded in its PDB (deeDebugger.hostSourceMap only if it was built elsewhere) rebuild + redeploy + re-attach

Two different edit loops, one attach

DEE debugging hot-reloads — the host recompiles your file on every trigger (see the mental model). Custom-business breakpoints bind against the already-deployed binary: there is no hot-reload — rebuild in Debug, redeploy with cmf dev local stack up, then re-attach (see the prerequisites). The single attach carries both source maps, so you can hold breakpoints in both at the same time. (Enable DEE Debug Mode is still what makes the host run your local DEE file; business DLLs need no such registration.)

Platform code has no source

The host makes every Cmf.* assembly debuggable — platform (Cmf.Foundation.*, Cmf.*) as well as your Cmf.Custom.*. You only have source for your customization, so a breakpoint binds only in Cmf.Custom.*; stepping into product Cmf.* shows "no source available" (expected). Attach uses justMyCode: false, so Step Over to stay in your code. See DEE vs custom-business debugging → which assemblies are debuggable.

docs.title: How business breakpoints find your source
docs.text:
A portable PDB records the path of every source file as it was when the DLL was built, and the debugger opens that path. A local cmf build records your repo's absolute paths (cmf-cli sets no PathMap), for example /path/to/<project>/Cmf.Custom.Business/Cmf.Custom.Orchestration/Foo.cs. When VS Code sees your repo at that same path — the usual devcontainer and WSL layout — business breakpoints bind with no source map at all.

   path recorded in the PDB                         where your source is now
   ─────────────────────────────────────────       ─────────────────────────────────
   /path/to/proj/Cmf.Custom.Business/…/Foo.cs    =  /path/to/proj/…/Foo.cs       → binds, no map
   /agent/_work/proj/Cmf.Custom.Business/…/Foo.cs → map { "/agent/_work/proj": "${workspaceFolder}" }
  • Set deeDebugger.hostSourceMap only when the recorded root differs from where your source lives now: the DLL was built in another folder or container, on a CI agent, or inside a container at /src (how Critical Manufacturing builds the platform itself). Map the recorded root to your repo root.
  • Leave it empty to use the default { "/src": "${workspaceFolder}" }, which covers /src container builds and is a harmless no-op for everything else.
  • The recorded root is simply the repo's path on the machine or container that ran cmf build. Opening a sub-folder of the same repo doesn't matter — the recorded paths are absolute.

docs.title: Running it, step by step
docs.text:
Run DEE Debugger: Attach Debugger to MES Host — from the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P), the debug icon in the DEE Explorer title bar, or the Attach Debugger button in the dialog that follows Enable DEE Debug Mode. It's the same command everywhere. Before it attaches, the extension walks a few checks:

  1. C# extension must be installed (it ships with this extension); if it's missing you get an [Install C# extension] button.
  2. An environment must be selected; if none is, an [Switch Environment…] button takes you there. (No MES sign-in / token is needed for the attach itself — attach is lower-privilege than DEE debug mode. You still select an environment because that's how the extension knows which host to reach.)
  3. Attaching to a non-local host asks you to confirm the privileged-attach warning (Continue).
  4. The first time only, a prerequisites primer lists what makes a breakpoint bind, for DEE actions and for business code (the three business prerequisites are below). Choose Attach to go on, or Open guide to read the guide first (this cancels the attach). Once you have answered it with either button, it doesn't show again.
  5. On a containerized host, the extension probes for the Linux PDB prerequisite. If the host is unpatched you get a warning with Patch Host for Debugging, but the attach continues.

You're attached when the debug toolbar appears. Set breakpoints in your Cmf.Custom.* code — they bind when the deployed code runs. If none of your enabled breakpoints has bound 8 seconds after the attach, the extension shows the likely causes with Show Log / Open guide buttons (plus Patch Host for Debugging when the host is known to be unpatched). DEE breakpoints whose action hasn't run yet also count as unbound here.

docs.title: The three prerequisites
docs.text:
Custom-business attach has no code of its own on the host — it binds against whatever is deployed, so all three of these must already be true:

  1. The DLLs and PDBs are deployed into the host image. cmf dev local stack up builds the host image from the base MES image plus a copy of LocalEnvironment/BusinessTier, and recreates the host container when that image changed (it does after a new build) — it compiles nothing. That folder is the output of a Debug build: cmf build --test (its test step builds Debug) or dotnet build Cmf.Custom.Business/Business.sln. A plain cmf build builds Release into Cmf.Custom.Business/Release/ and does not change what stack up deploys. Recreating the container also removes vsdbg (and, on 11.x, the host patch) and drops DEE debug registrations — the extension offers each again. Attach itself does not build or deploy anything.
  2. The PDBs are portable-format. The debugger on a Linux host reads only portable PDBs. cmf build already emits portable PDBs for your DLLs. The host patch (Linux PDB prerequisite, #158143) is a different fix: it changes only how the host compiles DEE actions, not your DLLs' PDBs.
  3. The recorded source paths resolve — automatic when you build and debug at the same path; otherwise set deeDebugger.hostSourceMap (see above).

While paused, the whole host freezes exactly as with DEE debugging, and load-balanced / multi-replica environments need the same pinning.

docs.title: DEE vs custom-business debugging
docs.text: One command — DEE Debugger: Attach Debugger to MES Host — debugs both kinds of MES customization C#. It attaches the .NET debugger to the running MES host once, with a source map that covers both, so a breakpoint binds wherever the matching code runs.

docs.title: Which assemblies are debuggable — and which you have source for
docs.text:
The MES host makes every assembly whose name starts with Cmf. debuggable — it deploys PDBs for them all. That's two groups:

  • Platform — Cmf.Foundation.*, Cmf.*. Debuggable, but you normally have no source for it.
  • Your customization — Cmf.Custom.<tenant>.*. Debuggable and you have the source.

The attach binds a breakpoint to source only where the source exists locally. Your Cmf.Custom.* PDBs record the paths your build used — normally your own repo's paths, so they resolve directly (or through hostSourceMap when the DLL was built elsewhere). Platform PDBs record Critical Manufacturing's build paths (under /src/), which aren't in your repo, so they resolve to nothing: a breakpoint there won't bind, and stepping into product Cmf.* code shows "no source available." That's expected, not a failure — you can only meaningfully set breakpoints in code you have the source for.

Staying in your own code

The attach uses justMyCode: false (DEE debugging needs it), so Step Into can descend into product Cmf.* frames that have no source. Use Step Over (F10), or set your breakpoints inside your Cmf.Custom.* code, to stay in code you can see.

docs.title: The two edit loops
docs.text: DEE action Custom business DLL (Cmf.Custom.<tenant>.*) What runs Host compiles your local .cs while Debug Mode is on The deployed, pre-built assembly Prerequisite Enable DEE Debug Mode on the action (on MES 11.x Linux hosts, also the host patch, #158143) DLL + portable PDB deployed via cmf dev local stack up (the host patch does not change these PDBs) Source map DEE temp folder → your file (automatic) none needed when you build and debug at the same path; deeDebugger.hostSourceMap maps a different build root (default { "/src": "${workspaceFolder}" }) Change code Edit → save → re-trigger (hot reload) Edit → Debug build (cmf build --test or dotnet build) + cmf dev local stack up → re-attach (no hot reload) MES sign-in Needed to load/run actions Not needed for the attach itself

docs.title: How the one attach covers both
docs.text:
The attach builds a merged sourceFileMap — the DEE temp folder and the business map — so coreclr resolves each breakpoint against whichever PDB matches. Business PDBs whose recorded paths already exist on this machine need no entry at all:

sourceFileMap:
  /tmp/CriticalManufacturing/dee-debug  →  ${workspaceFolder}      # DEE actions (subfolders mirrored)
  /src                                   →  ${workspaceFolder}      # default business entry (container builds)

You don't choose "DEE attach" vs "business attach" — you attach once and set breakpoints wherever you need them. (Enable DEE Debug Mode is still separate: it's what makes the host run your local DEE file with hot reload; business DLLs need no such registration.)

docs.title: If a breakpoint won't bind
docs.text:
A hollow (unbound) breakpoint is the common first hurdle. Most likely, in order:

  1. Custom business: the deployed DLL/PDB is stale — rebuild in Debug (cmf build --test or dotnet build; a plain Release cmf build does not update LocalEnvironment/BusinessTier), run cmf dev local stack up, then re-attach.
  2. Custom business: the PDB isn't portable — rebuild the DLLs with portable PDBs and redeploy. (Patch Host for DEE Debugging does not help here: it only changes how the host compiles DEE actions.)
  3. Custom business: the source paths recorded in the PDB don't exist here — the DLL was built in another folder, container or on CI, or you are debugging a copy of the repo. Map that build root with deeDebugger.hostSourceMap, e.g. { "/path/used/at/build": "${workspaceFolder}" }.
  4. DEE action: Debug Mode isn't on for that action, you triggered it as a different user than your token's, or (MES 11.x Linux host) the host isn't patched.

See Debugging → Attaching for custom business debugging for the full flow, and Troubleshooting for symptoms.

docs.title: Editing and uploading actions
docs.text: This page covers the single-action editing loop: open, edit safely, save back to the MES, and deal with compile errors, versions, and conflicts. For bulk operations across your whole project, see Sync.

docs.title: Opening an action
docs.text:
Click an action in the DEE Explorer. The extension looks for <ActionName>.cs in your DEEs folders, subfolders included, and opens the right file:

  • You already have the file in the MES format (the generated markers): it opens in place, wherever it lives. If its code differs from the MES version, a notice offers Compare and Reload from MES. Opening never replaces your file with the MES version on its own.
  • You have the file in the cmf-cli DeeDevBase format: your file is not touched. A working copy opens instead (see DeeDevBase files: working copies).
  • You have no file yet: the extension downloads the action as <ActionName>.cs into your primary DEEs folder.

The DEEs folders are auto-detected: every folder that contains DeeDevBase.cs, one per Data package. You can also list them in the deeDebugger.deesFolder setting; the first one is the primary folder. A downloaded file is a complete, compilable C# file: using directives, a generated wrapper class, and — inside four marker comments — your action code and test condition.

If two Data packages both contain <ActionName>.cs, the extension doesn't guess: it lists both files and asks you to keep one, or to limit deeDebugger.deesFolder to one package. It also never overwrites a file of that name that has damaged markers; fix or move the file first.

If your workspace contains the standard Actions project (Cmf.Custom.Data/DEEs with its .csproj and DeeDevBase.cs), the C# extension gives you IntelliSense, navigation, and local squiggles on these files automatically.

docs.title: DeeDevBase files: working copies
docs.text:
Projects created with cmf-cli often keep DEEs in the DeeDevBase format (//---Start DEE Code--- markers and a DeeDevBase base class). The MES host can only debug the MES format, and it rewrites the file it debugs. So the extension never edits or debugs a DeeDevBase file directly:

  1. Opening the action creates a working copy in the MES format, with your file's code, under .dee-debug/ at the root of your workspace. The path below .dee-debug/ mirrors your file's path, so files in different packages never collide.
  2. You edit, save to the MES and debug the working copy, exactly like any other DEE file.
  3. After each successful Save Action to MES, the extension offers Write Back. It copies the code into your DeeDevBase file and keeps that file's layout and line endings. You can also run Write Code Back to Source File from the editor title or the action's right-click menu at any time.
  4. If you edit and save the DeeDevBase file itself, its code is copied into the working copy. With debug mode on, that change is pushed to the host as usual.

.dee-debug/ contains its own .gitignore, so working copies are never committed. It sits outside every DEEs folder, so cmf build never packages them. Commit only your DeeDevBase file.

docs.title: Creating a new action
docs.text:
Click ＋ New DEE Action… in the DEE Explorer title (or run it from the Command Palette). You are asked for:

  1. Name — a C# identifier (letters, digits, underscores; starts with a letter), unique on this MES. The host enforces the same rule, so invalid names are rejected before any call is made.
  2. Description (optional) and a classification — pick one already in use or type a new one.
  3. Whether to create and make effective (recommended) or create as draft.

The action is created exactly like the MES UI wizard does (enabled, the standard starter template, return true; as the test condition), then downloaded and opened as <Name>.cs. One thing the extension does not do: add the action to an action group — do that in Administration → DEE Actions, otherwise the MES has no extension point from which to invoke it.

docs.title: Drafts: versions that are not effective
docs.text:
The MES keeps every version of an action, and at most one version is effective. Which version runs follows one rule: the effective version if there is one, otherwise the highest version. A freshly created action (either side) is stored as version 1 in state Active, not effective — and because no other version exists, the MES already runs it.

A version that isn't effective (a draft) is skipped only while another version is effective — for example a version you staged with Save as New Version… (keep current effective). The flip side: while no version is effective, a version staged later takes over immediately. That is why it pays to make a version effective.

The tree shows a draft row with a not effective (Active) badge and a warning-coloured icon, and offers Make Version Effective (inline ✓ or right-click). Saving into a draft says whether the MES runs it and offers the same action.

docs.title: The marker contract: what you may and may not edit
docs.text:
Every downloaded file contains four marker lines — the action code first, then the test condition:

/** START OF USER-DEFINED CODE (DO NOT CHANGE OR DELETE THIS LINE!) **/
// … your action code …
/** END OF USER-DEFINED CODE (DO NOT CHANGE OR DELETE THIS LINE!) **/

/** START OF USER-DEFINED VALIDATION CODE (DO NOT CHANGE OR DELETE THIS LINE!) **/
// … your test condition (must end in a return statement, e.g. return true;) …
/** END OF USER-DEFINED VALIDATION CODE (DO NOT CHANGE OR DELETE THIS LINE!) **/

Only the code between a START and its END marker belongs to you. Everything else — the using block, the class declaration, the method signatures — is a wrapper the server generates and will regenerate.

Warning — this is the #1 way to lose work. Edits outside the markers are not uploaded (only the marker bodies are sent to the MES). And while debug mode is on, the host rewrites its copy of the file with a freshly generated wrapper whenever yours differs; the extension pulls that rewrite into your local file, discarding your out-of-marker edits (it tells you when it does). Never edit the wrapper, never delete, duplicate, or add text on a marker line. The extension checks the markers before every upload and refuses with a specific message if they are damaged; if that happens, don't repair by hand — copy your body code somewhere safe, run Reload Action from MES to restore a clean wrapper, and paste your code back inside the markers.

docs.title: Need another assembly? UseReference, not using
docs.text:
Since you can't touch the using block, reference additional assemblies from inside the action-code markers:

UseReference("Cmf.Navigo.BusinessObjects.dll", "Cmf.Navigo.BusinessObjects");

The first argument is the assembly, the second the namespace to import. This is the supported mechanism; a hand-added using line above the markers is exactly the edit the host's rewrite will erase.

Keep the exact spacing if you package DEEs with cmf build

The Data package's build step validates every DEE file and rejects a UseReference call with any whitespace beyond the single space after the comma — write it exactly as UseReference("x.dll", "y");. The MES host itself is not that strict, so code that compiles on the MES can still fail cmf build.

docs.title: What's in scope inside the markers
docs.text:
• Input — a Dictionary<string, object> carrying the operation's data.
  • Input["ServiceProvider"] — the DI service provider for resolving MES services.
  • In the validation block, you must end with a return of a boolean (whether the action code should run).

docs.title: The three ways to save
docs.text:
What you do What happens Ctrl+S (save the file) Saves locally only. The MES is untouched. The tree shows a pending upload badge on the action. (Exception: with debug mode ON, saving also pushes your file to the host for your executions only — see Debugging.) Save Action to MES (Compile & Save) — the cloud-upload icon on the action's row (hover), or the Command Palette Compiles your marker bodies on the MES and overwrites the current version of the action for all users. This is the normal "publish my change" step. Success is confirmed briefly in the status bar and the pending upload badge clears; if the saved version is a draft you are offered Make Effective. Save Action to MES as New Version… — right-click the action Compiles and saves as a new version of the action, leaving the previous version intact in the history. You choose whether the new version becomes effective (the one the MES actually runs) immediately, or is stored without activating it.

Versioning semantics in short: the MES keeps every version of an action; exactly one version is effective at a time. Save Action to MES updates, in place, the version you are working on: the one you opened (the effective one, or the draft when no version is effective yet) — or, after Save as New Version…, that new version. If it is a draft, you are offered Make Effective. Reload Action from MES puts you back on the version shown in the tree. Save as New Version… is the safer choice for significant changes on shared environments — it preserves a rollback point, and "save but don't make effective" lets you stage a change without changing behavior. Browse and diff old versions any time with Show Version History… (right-click the action); a staged Active version can be promoted from there with Make vN Effective.

docs.title: Compile errors
docs.text:
When the MES rejects your upload, the compile errors appear:

  • as entries in VS Code's Problems panel, mapped onto the correct lines of your local file (inside the right marker region), and
  • as squiggles in the editor.

Fix the code and upload again; a clean save clears the diagnostics. The raw server response is also written to the DEE Debugger output channel if you need the unmapped original.

docs.title: Concurrency conflicts (someone else changed it)
docs.text:
If the action changed on the MES after you loaded it — a colleague uploaded, or you edited it in the MES UI — your upload is refused and a dialog explains that the action was changed on the MES since it was loaded:

  • Overwrite — pushes your marker bodies over the newer server version (their wrapper is refetched, so only the bodies are at stake).
  • Cancel — leaves the server untouched, so you can open a diff first (see Sync: compare) or reload and re-apply your change.

Note: Before overwriting, consider Show Version History… to see what you'd be replacing — or use Save Action to MES as New Version… so nothing is lost.

docs.title: Reloading from the MES
docs.text:
Right-click → Reload Action from MES (or the discard icon on the row) replaces your local file with the server's current content. A confirmation dialog always comes first, because Reload discards any pending local changes. This is also the standard fix for a broken wrapper or damaged markers.

If the file is open with unsaved changes in the editor, reload (and sync download) will not silently clobber it — see dirty-editor protection.

For a DeeDevBase file, Reload replaces only the working copy. Use Write Code Back to Source File afterwards if your repository file should take the MES version too.

docs.title: Trying an action without side effects
docs.text:
Execute Action… (right-click the action) runs it ad hoc with a JSON input dictionary you provide:

  • Read-only execution runs the code without persisting side effects — good for a quick check.
  • Full execution behaves like the real thing and asks for confirmation first.

The result opens as a JSON report with the input, the decoded output, and the duration.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
An environment is a named connection profile: the MES address, how the extension reaches the MES host container, and that environment's own stored credentials. All connection configuration goes through environments — there are no loose "host address" settings. Exactly one environment is active at a time; no active environment means "not connected", and the DEE Explorer shows its welcome view.

You will typically have one environment per MES instance you work with: your local stack, a shared dev server, a test cluster.

docs.title: Creating environments
docs.text:
Three ways:

  • DEE Debugger: Discover Environments… — probes your machine for reachable MES stacks (local Docker, docker-in-docker devcontainers, local host processes), verifies each with an API ping, and lets you connect in one click. Try this first.
  • DEE Debugger: Add Environment… — a guided wizard for every supported connection type (listed below). Use this when discovery can't see your MES — remote machines, Kubernetes, unusual setups.
  • Editing the deeDebugger.environments setting directly (Settings → search "DEE Debugger" → edit in settings.json). Handy for copying a colleague's working profile — but remember that credentials are not in settings; each person sets their own token.

Note: If you used an earlier version of the extension with the old flat connection settings, those were migrated automatically into an environment named default, credentials included. Nothing to do.

docs.title: Switching, managing, testing
docs.text:
• Switch: click the MES: \<name> Status Bar item, or run DEE Debugger: Switch Environment…. The switcher shows which environments already have a stored token (a key icon) and which don't (a warning icon). Switching to an environment without a token prompts you for one.
┌─ Switch MES environment ───────────────────────────────┐
│ ✓ local        http://localhost · 🔑 token set         │
│   test-cluster https://mes-test… · ⚠ no token          │
│ ＋ Add environment…                                     │
│ 🔍 Discover environments…                              │
│ ⚙ Manage environments…                                 │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • Manage: DEE Debugger: Manage Environments… lets you edit any field, rename (stored credentials follow the new name automatically), or remove an environment (its stored credentials are wiped). Removing the active environment switches you to the first remaining one in the list (or disconnects you if none is left).
  • Test: DEE Debugger: Test Connection proves the address and the token with one API call and reports success or a specific failure. It does not exercise the container settings; Collect Support Bundle… probes those (its engineProbe line).

Switching environments is clean: open sessions and debug registrations belonging to the previous environment are dropped or deactivated, and the tree reloads with the new environment's data.

docs.title: Per-environment credentials
docs.text:
Each environment stores its own credentials in the operating system's secure storage — never in settings files, never in your repository.

Run DEE Debugger: Set Credentials… (or the Set Credentials button on the Explorer welcome view) any time to (re)choose how to authenticate — the method is always your choice:

  • Set Personal Access Token… — a long-lived token; best for daily work.
  • Set Access Token… — a bearer token copied from the browser DevTools; expires ~1 h.

Set Credentials…, both individual prompts, and Clear Credentials always apply to the active environment. Full copy-a-token steps: Getting started → provide a token.

Which token wins if both are stored

If both an access token and a PAT are stored, the access token is used. Setting a Personal Access Token auto-clears any stored access token, so a new PAT takes effect immediately — no need to Clear Credentials first. The one case that still bites: pasting a browser access token after a PAT — the access token wins, and it keeps winning after it expires (every call then fails with an auth error). Set the PAT again (that removes the access token), or run Clear Credentials and set the one you want.

docs.title: Which connection type am I? (decision tree)
docs.text:
After the name and the MES address, the wizard asks how the extension reaches your MES host container. Follow the tree — the terminal check that decides most cases is docker ps run in the same VS Code window you'll use the extension from.

Details for each branch:

1. Does your MES host run in a container at all? - No — it's a process on this machine (rare; e.g. running the host service directly): choose Local process. No container plumbing is involved; when you attach, you pick the host process in VS Code's process picker. - Yes: continue.

2. Run docker ps in the same VS Code window. Do you see the MES containers (custom_host or host, traefik, db, …)? - Yes: choose Docker (local). This is the simple case — host address is usually http://localhost, container name custom_host (cmf-cli stacks) or host (some other stacks). This is also what you get when you run VS Code inside the devcontainer that runs the stack — from in there, everything is local. - You see only one container, whose image is named vsc-…: your stack runs on a Docker daemon inside a devcontainer — continue to 3. - You see nothing, but the stack exists somewhere else: continue to 4.

3. Docker-in-docker (devcontainer) — the common cmf-cli setup. The stack was started with cmf dev local stack up inside a project devcontainer, so from outside that devcontainer, docker ps shows only the devcontainer itself and http://localhost doesn't answer. Nothing is broken — the stack just lives one layer deeper. Choose Docker-in-docker (devcontainer). The wizard asks for the devcontainer's name and runs every container command through it. As the MES address, enter the devcontainer's IP (e.g. http://172.17.0.2). Discover Environments… fills in both for you. To find name and IP yourself:

docker ps --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Image}}'        # the vsc-… image row is the devcontainer
docker inspect <name> --format '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}'

Warning — devcontainer names and IPs are volatile. The devcontainer's name is randomly generated on every rebuild, and its IP can change on every restart. If an environment that worked yesterday suddenly can't connect or can't reach the container, re-check both and update the environment (Manage Environments…). To stop the name churn permanently, pin a name in the project's devcontainer.json: "runArgs": ["--name", "my-mes-dev"].

An alternative that avoids all of this: open VS Code inside the devcontainer and use a plain Docker (local) environment from there.

4. The stack is on another machine or in a cluster: - A remote machine's Docker daemon you can reach via a Docker context or an ssh://… / tcp://… daemon address: choose Docker (remote) and provide the context name or daemon URL. - You're on Windows and the stack runs inside a WSL distribution (and you are not using VS Code's own WSL remoting): choose Docker inside WSL and name the distribution (or leave it empty for the default one). - Kubernetes: choose Kubernetes (kubectl) and give the target pod or deployment (and namespace). kubectl must be configured for the cluster in your shell. - OpenShift: choose OpenShift (oc) — same as Kubernetes but using the oc CLI and your oc login session. - Anything else — podman, nerdctl, an ssh wrapper script, a jump host: choose Custom engine command… and provide the command prefix the extension should run container operations through.

docs.title: Per-type setup notes
docs.text: Pick your type above, then read its notes here — they cover the prerequisites and the one-line check that proves the engine path works before you blame the extension.

docs.title: Local Docker
docs.text:
• Prerequisite: docker ps in the same environment VS Code runs in shows the MES containers.
  • Verify the engine path: docker exec custom_host echo ok
  • Fully verified topology — this and docker-in-docker are the setups the extension is routinely tested against.

docs.title: Docker-in-docker (devcontainer)
docs.text:
• See the volatility warning above (name/IP change on rebuild/restart).
  • Verify the engine path: docker exec <devcontainer> docker exec custom_host echo ok
  • Fully verified topology.

docs.title: Remote Docker
docs.text:
• Warning: hostAddress must be the remote machine's MES address (e.g. http://mes-dev.example:80) — not http://localhost, which points at your machine. The wizard pre-fills your current address; change it.

  • Prerequisite: the context or daemon URL works without interactive prompts — use ssh keys/agents, never passwords in the command. Check with: docker --context <name> ps or docker -H ssh://user@host ps
  • Expect noticeably slower debug-file pushes and host-rewrite checks over ssh links; operations time out after 30 s.

docs.title: Docker inside WSL (VS Code on Windows)
docs.text:
• Only needed when VS Code runs on Windows itself. If you use VS Code's WSL remoting (green corner badge says WSL), you are already inside WSL — use plain Docker (local) instead.
  • Verify: wsl -d <distro> docker ps from a Windows terminal shows the MES containers.

docs.title: Kubernetes (kubectl) and OpenShift (oc)
docs.text:
• k8sTarget takes anything kubectl exec/oc exec accepts, e.g. deployment/host -n mes-dev or a pod name plus -n <namespace>.
  • Verify the engine path: kubectl exec deployment/host -n mes-dev -- echo ok (or the oc equivalent; OpenShift also needs a live oc login session).

  • Warning — debugging needs SYS_PTRACE in the pod spec. Unlike Docker, there is no privileged-exec escape hatch on Kubernetes: if the host pod's securityContext doesn't grant the SYS_PTRACE capability, attaching the debugger will fail even though browsing, editing and uploading work fine. Ask whoever owns the deployment to add securityContext: { capabilities: { add: ["SYS_PTRACE"] } } to the host container (dev/test clusters only). If the container runs as a non-root user (the product host image does), the added capability is dropped on exec, so the pod also needs runAsUser: 0, or the node needs kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0. The extension checks this before attaching and names the missing piece.

  • vsdbg is installed into the pod's writable layer — a pod restart or redeploy removes it; the extension simply offers to install it again.

  • Warning — multiple host replicas break debugging. The debug registration lives in one replica's memory and your pushed file in one pod's filesystem, while a Service load-balances every request — so activation, file, trigger and debugger scatter across replicas and debugging "randomly works" (or fails with file-not-found compiles). While debugging, either scale down: kubectl scale deployment/host --replicas=1 -n <namespace>, or pin everything to one pod: kubectl port-forward pod/<host-pod> 8080:8080, set hostAddress to http://localhost:8080, point k8sTarget at that same pod, and trigger via Execute Action… (the MES UI still routes through the ingress). Details and diagrams: How debugging works.

docs.title: Local process
docs.text: • For a MES host running directly on your machine (no container). Debug source files are used in place — no copying, no sourcePathInHost; attaching opens VS Code's process picker.

docs.title: Using a bind mount instead of copying (useMount)
docs.text: Any Docker-based type can skip the file copying during debugging if the host container already bind-mounts your local DEEs folder: add a volume mapping your DEEs folder to a container path (e.g. in a compose override: volumes: ["<abs path to DEEs>:/mnt/dees"]), set sourcePathInHost to that container path and useMount to true in the environment. Debug-mode files are then shared directly — instant pushes, no streaming. Requires editing the stack definition and recreating the container, so most people stay with the default copying, which needs no stack changes. With useMount, only files inside the mounted (primary) DEEs folder can be debugged: DeeDevBase working copies under .dee-debug/ and files in other Data packages are outside the mount, and the extension stops with a message naming the file.

docs.title: Custom engine command
docs.text:
• Any docker-CLI-compatible prefix works (podman, nerdctl, ssh devbox docker, a wrapper script). The extension appends exec … to it for every container operation (files are streamed through exec too, never copied with cp).
  • Verify: <your command> exec custom_host echo ok from a terminal.
  • Same trust rule as everything on this page: the command runs on your machine.

Note on maturity: local Docker and docker-in-docker are exercised against live MES stacks continuously. Remote Docker, WSL, Kubernetes, OpenShift and custom engines use the exact same mechanics and are covered by automated tests, but have seen less real-world mileage — if you hit a rough edge on one of them, capture a support bundle (DEE Debugger: Collect Support Bundle…) and report it.

docs.title: What each field means
docs.text:
You normally never touch these — the wizard fills them — but Manage Environments… and settings.json expose them:

Field Meaning Default when omitted name The environment's display name. Also the key under which its tokens are stored. (required) hostAddress Base URL of the MES API — what you'd put in a browser, e.g. http://localhost or https://mes-test.example.com. http://localhost kind How the host runs: docker, kubernetes, or process. docker containerName Name of the MES host container. cmf-cli stacks use custom_host; some other stacks use host. custom_host k8sTarget For Kubernetes/OpenShift: the pod or deployment (with namespace) to exec into. — engineCommand The command prefix used for all container operations, replacing plain docker. Examples: ["docker","exec","-i","<devcontainer>","docker"] for docker-in-docker; ["docker","--context","remote1"]; ["wsl","-d","Ubuntu","docker"]; ["oc"]. plain docker / kubectl sourcePathInHost Directory inside the host container where debug-mode source files are placed. /tmp/CriticalManufacturing/dee-debug useMount If the container already bind-mounts your local DEEs folder, set true so files don't need to be copied in. false vsdbgPath Where the .NET debugger lives inside the container. /vsdbg/vsdbg

Warning: The engineCommand is executed on your machine. Only use environment profiles from sources you trust — this is also why the extension refuses to run in untrusted workspaces. Avoid embedding passwords in a custom engine command; use ssh keys or contexts instead.

docs.title: Verifying a new environment
docs.text: After creating an environment, run DEE Debugger: Test Connection. If it fails, the message tells you whether the problem is reaching the address (stack down, wrong address, WSL networking) or authentication (token missing/expired). The troubleshooting page maps each failure to a fix.

docs.title: If I enable debug mode, does it affect my colleagues?
docs.text:
No. DEE debug mode is per user: the MES host runs your local file's code only for operations executed under your user account. Everyone else keeps executing the stored database version, at full speed, with no idea you're debugging. The database version doesn't change until you explicitly run Save Action to MES.

Two caveats on shared instances:

  • While you're paused at a breakpoint, the whole host process is suspended — the MES freezes for everyone until you continue. Pause briefly.
  • Save Action to MES (as opposed to just saving the file) publishes for everyone — know which save you're doing.

docs.title: Why does my breakpoint never hit, even though the action runs?
docs.text:
Because debug mode is per-user, the execution must happen as the user your token belongs to. The classic miss: your token is for user A (say, the account whose PAT you generated), but you trigger the operation in the MES UI logged in as user B — B's execution runs the stored version, and your breakpoint stays cold. Trigger the operation logged in as the token's user, or use Execute Action… in VS Code (which always runs as your token's user).

Other causes, in order of likelihood: the action simply hasn't executed yet since you enabled debug mode (breakpoints show hollow and bind on first execution); a load balancer routed the execution to a different host instance; the host restarted and forgot the registration. Details in Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Do I need to upload before debugging my changes?
docs.text: No — that's the point. With debug mode on, saving the file (Ctrl+S) is enough: the host compiles your file on the next execution. Save Action to MES is only for publishing the finished change to everyone.

docs.title: Can I use this against production?
docs.text:
Never. Debug mode and debugger attach are development/test tools:

  • A breakpoint pause stops the entire MES for all users.
  • Attaching a debugger to the host process is highly privileged.
  • Debug mode changes which code executes for your user — on production data.

The extension warns before attaching to non-local addresses, but the real safeguard is you: keep production environments out of your environment list entirely.

docs.title: Why don't I see all actions in the tree (or in Sync)?
docs.text:
The DEE Explorer shows every action the MES reports, one row per action — the same list as Administration → DEE Actions. Two things can still make a row disappear:

  • Disabled actions are hidden by default. When any are hidden the tree shows a "N disabled actions hidden — click to show" row; click it (or run Toggle Show Disabled Actions, or set deeDebugger.showDisabledActions) to reveal them.
  • A text filter is active: a filled filter icon in the DEE Explorer's title means one is — click it and clear the text to restore the full tree.

Actions whose current version is not yet effective (a draft) are not hidden — they carry a not effective (Active) badge. Sync always covers every action the MES reports, including disabled actions and drafts.

docs.title: I created a DEE — does it run before I make it effective?
docs.text:
Yes. A newly created action is stored as version 1 in state Active, not effective, and the MES runs the effective version or, when none is effective, the highest version — so v1 runs. The not effective badge still matters: until a version is effective, a version staged later (Save as New Version…) takes over immediately. Right-click → Make Version Effective (or the ✓ inline icon) fixes the version that runs. New DEE Action… asks this up front, and a Sync upload that creates actions offers it at the end of the batch.

If a new action doesn't run at all, check that it is enabled and belongs to an action group — membership is configured in the MES UI.

docs.title: Why does the same action appear more than once?
docs.text: An action can belong to several action groups; it appears under each of them. It's the same action — editing or toggling debug from any of its entries affects all of them.

docs.title: What's the difference between "Save to MES" and "Save as New Version"?
docs.text: Save Action to MES (Compile & Save) overwrites, in place, the version you are working on — the one you opened (effective, or the draft when none is effective), or the version you last created with Save as New Version…. When that version is a draft you are offered Make Effective; the message says whether the MES runs that draft (it does when no other version is effective). Reload Action from MES returns you to the version shown in the tree. Save Action to MES as New Version… creates a new version and lets you choose whether it becomes effective immediately — the previous version stays in the history as a rollback point. Use new versions for significant changes on shared environments. Show Version History… lists every version (effective one marked) and can diff any of them against your local file. See versioning semantics.

docs.title: Two of us edited the same action — what happens?
docs.text: Whoever uploads second gets a conflict dialog: the action changed on the MES since they loaded it, with the choice to Overwrite or cancel and reconcile first. Bulk sync uploads similarly refuse entries that changed server-side since your last compare. Nothing is silently lost — but agree with your team on who owns an action, or use new versions. Details: concurrency conflicts.

docs.title: Can several people debug on the same dev instance?
docs.text: Yes — debug registrations are per (user, action), so two developers can debug different (or even the same) actions with their own files, each seeing only their own code changes. The shared limits: only one debugger can be attached to the host process at a time, and anyone's breakpoint pause freezes the instance for all.

docs.title: Where do the .cs files go? Do I have to commit them?
docs.text: Into your workspace's DEEs folder — auto-detected (every folder containing DeeDevBase.cs, or every folder named DEEs that contains a .csproj), configurable via deeDebugger.deesFolder (one folder or a list), falling back to a .dees/ folder. Existing files are used where they are, subfolders included; only new actions are downloaded, into the first folder. DeeDevBase-format files get a working copy under .dee-debug/, which is never committed (see working copies). Committing them is optional but recommended: with the standard Actions project you get IntelliSense, reviewable diffs, and the sync workflow.

docs.title: Is the tool slow with big environments?
docs.text: Loading the tree takes two requests (all groups and all actions), sent in parallel. Environments with thousands of actions take a few seconds to refresh but stay responsive (loading is in the background). Use Filter Actions… rather than scrolling; opening, uploading, and debugging single actions is unaffected by environment size. If a refresh feels stuck while a debug session is active, remember a paused host answers nothing.

docs.title: Where are my tokens stored? Is anything sent anywhere?
docs.text: Tokens live in your operating system's secure credential store (via VS Code's secret storage), scoped per environment — never in settings files or your repo. This covers both credential kinds: a browser-copied access token and a Personal Access Token. The extension collects no telemetry and talks only to the MES hosts you configure. Logs and the support bundle automatically redact credentials.

docs.title: Does it work on Windows / macOS / Linux / WSL?
docs.text: Yes — anywhere VS Code and (for containerized hosts) the docker CLI work. The one platform note concerns installing the debugger (vsdbg) into the host. When the host container has no curl or wget — true of MES 11.x host images; MES 12 images have curl — the extension downloads vsdbg locally and streams it in, which needs local bash and tar. That path isn't available on plain Windows without WSL. One current limitation: in a multi-root workspace, only the first folder is searched for the DEEs project.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
This page takes you from nothing to a loaded DEE Explorer tree — typically in under 10 minutes. For a full guided session that ends with a breakpoint hit, continue with the tutorial afterwards.

Tip: the same steps are available inside VS Code as an interactive walkthrough with a button per step — run DEE Debugger: Open Getting Started (also linked from the DEE Explorer's welcome view and Help → Welcome). This page is the long form with screenshots and troubleshooting.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• VS Code 1.90 or newer.
  • The extension VSIX (dee-debugger-<version>.vsix), from your team's usual distribution channel or CI builds.
  • The Microsoft C# extension (ms-dotnettools.csharp). It provides the .NET debugger the extension uses. It is declared as a dependency, so VS Code installs it automatically with the VSIX when it has Marketplace access; on an offline machine, install it first. C# Dev Kit also works — it includes the C# extension.
  • A running MES development or test instance you are allowed to change — for example a local stack started with cmf dev local stack up in your customization project.
  • A MES user account with permission to use DEE Actions (the same account you use in Administration → DEE Actions in the MES UI).
  • The docker CLI available in the same environment VS Code runs in, if your MES host runs in a container (it almost always does). Quick check: open VS Code's integrated terminal and run docker ps.

Note: The extension only works in trusted workspaces. If VS Code shows the Workspace Trust prompt when you open your folder, choose Trust.

docs.title: Step 1 — Install the extension
docs.text:
Get the .vsix from the project's GitHub Releases page (or a CI build artifact). Then either drag it onto the Extensions view, or from a terminal:

code --install-extension dee-debugger-<version>.vsix

Then run Developer: Reload Window (the extension host only picks up a new build after a reload). A new DEE Debugger icon appears on the Activity Bar.

Upgrading or replacing a pilot build

--install-extension replaces an older version in place. If an internal pilot build with a higher version number is installed (early testers had a 0.3.0 pilot), VS Code may treat the release as a downgrade — add --force, or uninstall first:

code --uninstall-extension criticalmanufacturing.dee-debugger
code --install-extension dee-debugger-<version>.vsix

Environments and stored tokens survive both paths (they are keyed by the extension id). Working inside WSL or a Remote-SSH / devcontainer window: run the command in that remote's terminal so the extension lands on the remote side, where docker is.

docs.title: Step 2 — Open a folder
docs.text:
The extension needs a workspace folder to store the .cs files it downloads.

  • Best: open your customization project — the folder containing Cmf.Custom.Data/DEEs. The extension auto-detects the DEEs folders (it looks for DeeDevBase.cs, or a folder named DEEs that contains a .csproj), including their subfolders and every Data package, and the Actions project gives you full C# IntelliSense for free.
  • Also fine: any folder. Downloaded files then go into a .dees/ subfolder. You can point the extension somewhere specific later with the deeDebugger.deesFolder setting.

docs.title: Step 3 — Discover your environment
docs.text:
1. Click the DEE Debugger icon on the Activity Bar. Since you are not connected yet, the DEE Explorer shows a welcome view with the next step as a button. (The welcome view adapts: not connected → Discover / Add; environment without a token → Set Credentials; connected but nothing loaded → Refresh / Show Output Log.)
  2. Click Discover Environments (also available from the Command Palette as DEE Debugger: Discover Environments…).
  3. The extension probes for MES stacks it can reach — a local Docker stack, a stack inside a devcontainer, or a local host process — and verifies each candidate by pinging its API. Reachable ones are pre-checked.
  4. Select your stack and choose Connect.

If nothing is discovered, your setup probably needs a manually configured environment — see Environments, in particular the connection decision tree.

docs.title: Step 4 — Provide a token
docs.text:
The extension authenticates to the MES with a token, stored securely per environment (in your OS keychain via VS Code — never in settings files). When you connect to an environment without a stored token, the Set Credentials… chooser opens automatically — pick how you want to authenticate:

┌─ Authenticate to 'local' ──────────────────────────────┐
│ Choose how to provide credentials                      │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 🔑 Set Personal Access Token…                          │
│    Long-lived token from the Security Portal — best     │
│    for daily work.                                      │
│ 📋 Set Access Token…                                    │
│    Bearer token copied from the browser DevTools —      │
│    expires after ~1 hour.                               │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Personal Access Token Access token (browser) Command Set Personal Access Token… Set Access Token… Where from Security Portal → your user page Browser DevTools → Network tab Lifetime Long-lived ~1 hour (Security Portal stacks) Best for Daily work Quick start / no PAT page

Recommended: Personal Access Token

PATs are long-lived, so you set them once. Generate one in the MES Security Portal → your user security page → Personal Access Tokens, copy it, then run DEE Debugger: Set Personal Access Token… and paste it.

docs.title: Copying an access token from the browser
docs.text:
If your setup has no Security Portal PAT page, reuse the token your browser session already has:

  1. Log in to the MES UI in your browser, then open DevTools (F12) → Network tab.
  2. Perform any data operation (for example, open a Material).
  3. Click a POST request to /api/... and find the Authorization: Bearer … header.
  4. Right-click → Copy value and paste without the Bearer prefix into DEE Debugger: Set Access Token….

Access tokens expire after 1 hour

On Security Portal stacks — including the standard local development stack — a browser access token dies after an hour, and every operation then fails with an authentication error until you paste a fresh one. This is the single most common problem people hit; a PAT avoids it entirely. See Expired tokens.

Pasted the wrong kind?

Paste a PAT into the Set Access Token… prompt by mistake and the extension recognizes it, stores it as a PAT, and tells you so. Manual copy-selection truncates these 1–2 KB tokens — always use right-click → Copy value.

docs.title: Step 5 — Watch the tree load
docs.text:
After the token is stored, the DEE Explorer loads:

DEE EXPLORER                      ↻  ＋  ⌕  🐞   …      ← title bar: Refresh · New DEE Action ·
● Connected · local                                         Filter · Attach; the rest under …
  3 disabled actions hidden — click to show
▾ MaterialManagement                                   2   ← group rows show their action count
  ▾ MaterialManagementOrchestration                    2
    ▾ CreateMaterial                                   2   ← each dot-separated part is a level
      ▾ Pre                                            2
          SetDefaultWarehouse    DEBUG · pending upload · v2
          ValidateLotSize                            v3
  OrphanAction                                        v1   ← ungrouped actions sit at the root
  Tutorial_MyFirstDee     not effective (Active) · v1   ← a draft (runs: no version is effective)
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
MES: local · 🐞 1                                          ← Status Bar: environment + debug count
  • A Connected · \<environment name> row with a green plug icon at the top confirms where you point; click it to switch. Below it, an "N disabled actions hidden" row appears when the default filter hides anything — click it to show them.
  • Action Groups appear as a folder hierarchy (dot-delimited names become nested levels) with the number of actions they hold; actions are the leaves. Ungrouped actions sit at the root.
  • Badges on an action row, in order of urgency: DEBUG (debug mode on; the row icon also turns into a coloured bug), pending upload (saved locally, not yet on the MES), not effective (Active) (a draft: it runs while no version is effective, but a version staged later would take over — right-click → Make Version Effective), disabled, and the version number.
  • Hover a row for the inline actions: Enable/Disable DEE Debug Mode, Save to MES, Reload from MES, and Make Version Effective on drafts. Right-click for the rest (new version, history, execute, Open in MES UI).
  • The title bar keeps four extension icons — Refresh, New DEE Action…, Filter, Attach Debugger — next to VS Code's own Collapse All, and puts Switch Environment, Sync, Expand All, Show Disabled, Show Output Log, Collect Support Bundle and Open Getting Started under the … menu.
  • The Status Bar shows MES: \<environment name> and, while any action is in debug mode, a bug icon with the count.

Click any action to open its code — and read Editing and uploading before you edit anything: only the code between the marker comments is yours.

If the tree stays empty or an error appears, run DEE Debugger: Test Connection from the Command Palette and see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: How DEE debugging works (client + host internals)
docs.text: You don't need this page to use the debugger — debugging.md covers that. Read this when you want to understand why it behaves the way it does: why breakpoints are per-user, why a host restart loses debug mode, why the host sometimes rewrites your file, and why multi-replica clusters need pinning.

docs.title: The moving parts
docs.text: Key asymmetry: the database is never involved in debug mode. The registration lives only in the host process's memory, and the code the host runs for you comes only from the registered file.

docs.title: The full loop, step by step
The registration's lifecycle (and why restarts matter)
docs.text: The extension detects the Lost state by comparing its local badge with the server's per-user IsInDebugMode after every refresh — the host itself never announces it.

docs.title: What the host actually does (for the curious)
docs.text:
1. Registration is four lines in the host: build an ActionDebugInfo{Id, Name, path} and put it in a per-tenant in-memory dictionary keyed by your user account. The IsInDebugMode/SourceFilePath you see in API responses are computed from that dictionary, not database columns.
  2. Every execution checks that dictionary for the calling user. Hit → unconditional recompile from your file. Miss → the cached Release build of the database version.
  3. The debug compile re-extracts your two marker bodies from the file and regenerates the full wrapper (usings come from your UseReference(...) calls, never from the file's using lines). If the regenerated wrapper differs from your file, the host rewrites your file; the extension's watcher pulls that back into your editor. Then Roslyn compiles the file with a file-backed syntax tree, embedded source, and emits <guid>.dll + <guid>.pdb whose document paths are your file — which is exactly what lets the attached debugger bind your breakpoints.
  4. Pausing at a breakpoint suspends every thread of the host — all users, the UI, everything — until you continue. This is normal .NET debugging, and the core reason debug mode is a development/test-only feature.

docs.title: Multi-replica clusters: why pinning is mandatory
docs.text:
Because the registration is one replica's memory and the file is one pod's filesystem, four things must land on the same replica: the ActivateDebugMode call, the pushed file, the triggering execution, and the attached debugger. A load balancer scatters them:

With N replicas you get roughly a 1-in-N chance per trigger that everything aligns — experienced as "debugging randomly works", plus file-not-found compile errors when the registration and the file land on different replicas.

Fix, in order of preference:

  1. Scale the host to one replica in the dev/test namespace while debugging: kubectl scale deployment/host --replicas=1 -n <namespace>. (A hit breakpoint freezes the whole host anyway — multi-replica debugging has no upside.)
  2. Pin everything to one pod: kubectl port-forward pod/<host-pod> 8080:8080, set the environment's hostAddress to http://localhost:8080, and set k8sTarget to that same pod. Then trigger via Execute Action… (which uses your pinned address) rather than the MES UI, whose requests still go through the ingress.

The same applies to any classic load-balanced deployment — the original Visual Studio add-in documentation carried the equivalent warning.
